item.title: CIS Tender 12 seeks 5 GW of solar or wind generation across the NEM, excludes NSW
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: The federal government's Capacity Investment Scheme Tender 12 that seeks up to 5 GW of new renewable energy generation across the National Electricity Market, excluding New South Wales, has opened on 27 November 2026.
item.content:encoded:
The Capacity Investment Scheme (CIS) Tender 12 that seeks up to 5 GW of new renewable energy generation across the National Electricity Market (NEM), excluding New South Wales (NSW), opened 27 November 2026.

Federal Assistant Minister for Climate Change and Energy Josh Wilson said the CIS gives investors confidence to build the new energy Australia needs.

“This next tender will unlock up to 5 GW of new renewable generation to help power Australian homes and businesses for decades to come,” Wilson said.

Developer Rating Scheme

It is now mandatory for CIS applicants to participate in the Developer Rating Scheme (DRS), introduced on 29 October 2026, which requires proponents to start the DRS assessment process before bidding.

The DRS is designed to give landholders, councils, and local communities transparent information on developer conduct, character, capability, capacity, capital, and community engagement.

“Clean energy projects work best when they are developed with communities, not simply in communities,” Wilson said.

“Requiring participation in the Developer Rating Scheme will give landholders and local communities clearer information about developers and their track record.”

First Nations Set Aside

Proponents must also commit to at least 5% First Nations equity and/or an equivalent revenue-sharing under the First Nations Equity and Revenue Sharing Set Aside (FNERSSA) scheme, that reserves portions of CIS tenders for projects with First Nations economic participation.

The FNERSSA scheme was piloted in CIS Tender 9, where 500 MW was set aside within a 5 GW renewable generation tender, and CIS Tender 10, where 500 MW / 2 GWh was set aside within a 4 GW / 16 GWh dispatchable capacity and battery storage tender.

A First Nations Set Aside allocation of 500 MW will be available to Tender 12 proponents that commit to entering into a First Nations sharing arrangement that meets the qualification requirements set out in the tender guidelines.

“The dedicated First Nations Set Aside will create more opportunities for First Nations communities to share in the long-term benefits of Australia’s energy transformation,” Wilson said.

CIS Tender – NEM Generation 12 registrations close 22 January 2027, with successful proponents announced in June 2027.

Successful outcomes from CIS Tender 9 – NEM Generation, 5 GW are expected in early December 2026.

NSW Roadmap tenders

Projects with generation assets located in the NSW region of the NEM are not eligible to participate in CIS Generation – Tender 12 but can refer to future NSW Roadmap tenders.

The NSW Roadmap Tender 10 is expected to open for bids before the close of 2026 and seeks 2.5 GW of generation capacity across NSW, for either a generation long-term energy service agreement (LTESA) or a hybrid generation LTESA.

item.title: Walking the walk is more important than the climate talk
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Nearly a quarter of countries have breached the Paris Agreement by not submitting new nationally determined contributions to the United Nations. This isn’t a one-off, or just exclusive to governments. Recent research found nearly 40% of companies missed or abandoned 2020 climate targets with no consequences.
item.content:encoded:
We’ve seen thousands of organisations, institutions and even countries pledge their sustainability commitments. Yet little is known of what has actually been achieved, because setting a credible sustainability target is the first, and easiest, hurdle to jump.

The hard work comes when the declarer of a goal has to figure out a way to meet it.

Thankfully Australia is on track in its commitment to net-zero by 2050 – but that’s not to say the road to meeting commitments is simple.

Loud ambition meets operational reality

For years, sustainability progress was measured through loud commitments – credible targets, clear roadmaps and reported progress, all of which were treated as signs of real momentum. This work built an important initial layer, but when it came to legitimate transitions, it has become a little murky.

The hard truth is that execution isn’t always the next step. It should be, but instead it is often where trade-offs start to surface.

First, there needs to be capital investments because electrification, cleaner energy and supply lines aren’t free. But this is a tough trade-off for executives.

It is often the executive team that must make trade-off decisions about assets, energy, suppliers and capital every day, and whether each decision aligns with a business’ bottom line.

Sustainability runs through the operating model

Companies willing to invest in clean energy aren’t just reaching sustainability goals; they’re working towards operational security, resilience, cost control and competitiveness.

Energy efficiency is no longer an aloof target or a ‘nice to have’. It is part of a broader resilience strategy helping businesses manage volatile pricing, supply chain uncertainty and operational risk, and from a business standpoint, there’s no better time to say goodbye to a reliance on fossil fuels.

Organisations with strong emissions visibility are seeing just how beneficial the transition can be when data shows you how to navigate regulatory pressures and market risk. Data allows leaders to embed sustainability into core business decisions, so that they can make better decisions.

For many organisations, the answer to these questions is still too fragmented to answer them with confidence. That’s a major business and sustainability barrier.

Potential is not performance

That evidence gap is where a lot of transition plans start to come unstuck. Energy, operations, maintenance, finance and sustainability teams are still working in their own separate systems, so each one only sees part of the picture.

Cost, carbon and operational performance are rarely looked at side by side which means blind spots can creep in, decisions get bogged down, and the cost of running inefficiently quietly adds up.

Real-time data matters because it helps close that gap. It brings trade-offs into view earlier, before capital is committed and options narrow.

But technology doesn’t hand you efficiency on a plate. Software chews through energy, artificial intelligence (AI) workloads are notoriously power-hungry, and data centres leave a footprint of their own. Any digital sustainability strategy worth its salt has to reckon with both sides of the ledger.

Evidence is often the toughest nut to crack in sustainability. The organisations getting it right are the ones focused not just on sustainability itself, but on how they measure it, and they’re making calls faster and dodging the usual bottlenecks as a result. When data is shared early, everyone’s on the same page by the time a trade-off needs to be made.

For leaders, the question isn’t which shiny new tool to roll out. It’s whether their people have the data, the authority and the incentives to act on the trade-offs that tool brings to light.

*

Author: AVEVA Vice President , Pacific David Such

item.title: Beyond silicon’s ceiling: The acceleration of perovskite solar
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Perovskite tandem manufacturers are moving past laboratory efficiency records to prioritise long-term field durability, bankability, and gigawatt-scale commercial production.
item.content:encoded:
Beyond standard single-junction silicon solar technologies, which are rapidly approaching their theoretical efficiency ceilings, the solar industry is turning to perovskite tandem architectures to unlock the next wave of energy yield and cost reductions.

At a panel session during Solar Manufacturing USA 2026, hosted by pv magazine USA, industry executives and researchers outlined how leading developers are taking perovskite-on-silicon tandems out of the laboratory and into commercial deployment.

Ralf Preu, director of photovoltaics at Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE, put the technology shift into historical perspective, reflecting on how far solar manufacturing has progressed.

“My journey is more than 30 years in PV,” Preu noted, recalling an early visit to a 10 MW plant in Camarillo, California, which was once one of the three largest production sites in the world. “It’s great to see that with all the production sites, what was manufactured there in a year, we have it now in a few hours.”

Preu highlighted the absolute physical necessity of moving past single-junction silicon, pointing out that industrial cell efficiencies have drawn dangerously close to theoretical boundaries.

“The efficiency limit for silicon single junction is 29.4%. That’s the maximum you can get out of a solar cell, and we are now – with the announcement of Longi – we are so close to that with 28.1%. And even if we look at the module, we are at 26.4% efficiency. Obviously, there is not much to squeeze out of that theoretical efficiency limit anymore.”

To break through this wall, multijunction architectures are essential. “The main objective, how to get beyond that, is to go for tandems, and if you look at the potential of a perovskite-silicon tandem two-junction cell, this is at 43.2%, so 14% absolute more,” Preu explained, adding that triple junctions can eventually push theoretical efficiencies beyond 50%.

While early-stage perovskite research focused heavily on efficiency records, current efforts prioritise bankability, long-term outdoor stability, and scalable manufacturing. Presentations from Oxford PV, Caelux, Swift Solar, Tandem PV, and CubicPV highlighted distinct approaches to bridging the gap between gigawatt-scale production and commercial reliability.

Commercial shipments

The industry milestone of sending commercial perovskite products to field installations is no longer a distant projection. Dr. Laura Miranda, chief strategy officer at Oxford PV, detailed the company’s transition from early R&D to active manufacturing at its pilot line in Brandenburg an der Havel, Germany.  

Oxford PV’s product strategy centres on its Centauri and Pegaso series modules, targeting mainstream utility installations alongside lightweight specialty applications.

Addressing the company’s broader approach, Miranda emphasised a fundamental shift in priorities. “Efficiency world records are not a product. We fail fast, learn fast, and keep going. We’ve been doing that for more than a decade, so we know what doesn’t work very well.”

Looking ahead, Oxford PV targets 25% module efficiency with a 10-year lifespan guarantee in 2026, stepping up to a 20-year lifespan guarantee by 2027.

“We never release a product that doesn’t come with a lifetime guarantee,” Miranda stated. “2027 is the critical point. At that point, it makes sense to upscale this technology to mass production because the LCOE makes sense.”

To expand its global footprint, Oxford PV plans to pair direct manufacturing with technology licensing models for module producers.

“We don’t use IP to block competitors,” Miranda added. “We think there is space for everybody, and what we want to do is align, create partnerships, and license our IP to accelerate deployment into different markets.”

Active glass

While building a complete monolithic tandem cell remains an industry focus, alternative integration methods seek to reduce manufacturing complexity for established module makers. Developers are pursuing simpler pathways that add perovskite absorption without requiring panel manufacturers to retool their fundamental silicon operations.

One strategy coats the panel’s protective front glass with a light-absorbing perovskite layer. Caelux presented its Solar Amplified glass platform, which allows module producers to replace standard front glass with power-producing glass.

Aaron Thurlow, CCO of Caelux, explained that this drop-in replacement boosts power output across passivated emitter and rear contact (PERC), tunnel oxide passivated contact (TOPCon), heterojunction (HJT), and back-contact architectures while leaving underlying cell lines untouched.

Another strategy relies on mechanically stacking a perovskite layer over a silicon cell and wiring them together inside the junction box. Operating out of a 40 MW commercial demonstration facility in Fremont, California, Tandem PV scales this approach using off-the-shelf equipment and standard 1,200 mm glass widths.

“In thin films, it’s the width that kills you,” said Dr. Colin Bailie, CTO of Tandem PV. “We focused on this 1,200 mm form factor in order to reduce all of that risk to scale in this pilot line.”

By avoiding internal cell re-engineering, these stacked modules mount on standard racking just like conventional panels.

“No power electronics, no MLPEs, no fuss,” Bailie added. “You can install it just how you plan to install your standard silicon modules on your single-axis trackers – same frames, same voltages, just a little bit more current.”

Tandem PV reported a 27.6% pilot module efficiency on a 0.7 square meter area with under 1% annual degradation. The company plans to ship field test kits in late 2026, targeting full bankability reports in 2027 ahead of a GW-scale U.S. plant in 2028.

HJT as a foundation

A central point of discussion was selecting the optimal silicon bottom-cell architecture for monolithic two-terminal tandems. Dr. Joel Jean, CEO and co-founder of Swift Solar, argued that silicon HJT provides the best foundation for perovskite top cells.

“HJT today is the foundation for multiple generations of technology in this industry … where you can boost that efficiency ceiling up to the mid-40s, and then triple junctions on top of that same foundation, which gets you up to about 50%,” Jean said.

Swift Solar recently acquired key assets and IP from Meyer Burger to establish U.S.-based HJT cell and module production.

“We acquired a combination of the global IP portfolio – over $200 million – but the strongest HJT positions, as well as over 2 GW of cell manufacturing equipment … and the corps of Meyer Burger, including the leadership,” Jean explained.

“So we’re moving from having proven HJT lines, with the legacy of Meyer Burger, toward a 2 GW U.S. factory. I think this is the first time we’re talking about this really in public.”

Swift Solar’s phased commercial strategy involves scaling a 2 GW U.S. facility producing high-efficiency HJT modules first, providing a bankable foundation before transitioning lines into monolithic 2T tandems.

“The most important thing to remember here is that this is the same supplier, the same line, the same module formats – G12R half-cut – going into the market with more power with each generation,” Jean added.

Durability concerns

To compete with legacy silicon modules backed by 25- to 30-year warranties, perovskite manufacturers must demonstrate long-term durability under harsh environmental conditions. Laureen Sanderson, CCO of CubicPV, stressed that perovskite commercialisation depends on an uncompromising quality focus.

“Everything that Cubic does is focused on durability first,” Sanderson stated. “We know perovskites work. We’ve seen a lot of world records over the last few years … But we need them to last. If you have a world record efficiency in perovskite, it doesn’t mean a single thing if that material is not going to last in the field.”

Sanderson noted that standard IEC qualification tests were designed for silicon packaging and fail to capture the dynamic ways perovskites interact with stress factors.

“There is no durability playbook today for perovskite. If someone passes IEC tests in perovskite, it means that they have passed the minimum test for packaging. That’s a pretty easy box to check … ISOS guidelines are not sufficient,” she explained. “Perovskites are a pretty finicky, fickle material. Everything interacts: composition, chemistry, interfaces, processing, environmental factors … What Cubic has done is build the machines to answer the questions that others cannot.”

(Note: ISOS stands for International Summit on Organic PV Stability. Guidelines established by ISOS are a set of tests developed by researchers working on much older, lab-scale devices.)

Next steps

What ties these distinct corporate strategies together is a shared industry-wide triumph over perovskite’s historically notorious weakness: field degradation.

A decade ago, early lab-scale perovskite devices degraded within minutes or hours when exposed to ambient moisture, heat, and ultraviolet radiation.

Now, field survival of perovskites has increased by orders of magnitude, with current pilot modules surviving thousands of hours under accelerated stress testing and projecting 20- to 25-year operational field lifetimes.

This milestone in material stability is what makes every commercial approach showcased during the session possible. Whether through Caelux’s drop-in active glass, Tandem PV’s mechanically stacked modules, Swift Solar’s HJT-based 2T cells, or Oxford PV’s commercial shipments, the entire industry is converging on a single reality.

Moderated by Ralph Romero of Black & Veatch, the session made clear that bankability remains the final hurdle before GW deployment. However, with multi-thousand-hour test data secured, degradation rates under 1%, and GW-scale factories poised to break ground in the U.S., perovskite tandems are actively entering the commercialisation stage.

item.title: Electric truck start up targets ‘missing middle’ of global road freight sector
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Melbourne-based electric trucking technology company DUKA Tec, is targeting the 'missing middle' of the global freight sector to electrify light and medium trucks that move goods around cities.
item.content:encoded:
Melbourne-based electric trucking technology company DUKA Tec, is targeting the ‘missing middle’ of the global freight sector to electrify light and medium trucks that move goods around cities.

It is currently raising $10 million (USD 6.6 million) from global investors to scale its artificial-intelligence (AI)-driven electric drivetrain technology and software platform.

Already holding assembly partnership agreements in Australia, the US and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), it also plans to establish electric truck assembly operations in Melbourne.

The company’s licensing model enables truck makers to electrify the models they already build, helping legacy truck manufacturers electrify faster and at a fraction of the cost of developing their own electric drivetrains and systems.

DUKA Tec Founder and Chief Executive Officer Tony Fairweather said the company is focused on accelerating the electrification road freight that established manufacturers have been slow to electrify due to scale and R&D challenges.

“Our technology is light, low cost and efficient, and designed specifically for urban delivery trucks,” Fairweather said.

“The reality is many truck makers simply don’t have the volumes to justify developing electric drivetrains for every model. We supply the electric drivetrain, the software and the support, and the truck maker sells the truck. It means they can bring their models to market as electric, much faster and cost effectively.”

DUKA Tec estimates around 250 truck makers already produce around 3,500 models, ranging from 4.5- tonne delivery trucks to metropolitan prime movers, that will all need to be electrified.

Artificial intelligence

DUKA Tec-enabled trucks are fully connected, with over-the-air software updates, real-time telematics and AI-driven prognostics built on over a decade of fleet data.

The AI platform monitors vehicle health, optimises fleet performance and maximises uptime, and route planning is integrated into fleet systems.

The company said DUKA Tec gives operators the full benefits of connectivity while keeping them in control of their data.

“The future of electric trucks is connectivity. DUKA Tec enabled trucks are not only more efficient, but they are also smarter and more secure. We’re providing a fully connected solution that drives productivity and safety, and one that fleets can trust,” Fairweather.

Fairweather said DUKA Tec is generation two, and follows his previous SEA Electric company, which put more than 900 electric trucks on the road before being acquired.

“DUKA Tec builds on [SEA Electric] with a capital-light licensing model, AI-driven technology and software we’ve rebuilt from the ground up,” Fairweather said.

Adding that electric trucks are cheaper to operate than diesel over the life of the vehicle, Fairweather said truck makers haven’t had the ability to electrify proven models, and this has meant they have increasingly been left behind as the world turns to electric options.

“DUKA Tec’s licensing model and partnerships with assembly plants changes the economics of electrification for the world’s truck manufacturers,” Fairweather said.

“The question now is how fast we can electrify this segment, with the connectivity and control fleet operators want. With proven technology, an experienced team and a capital-light model, DUKA Tec has the potential to scale quickly, delivering cheaper, cleaner freight and a more secure, independent for transport, in Australia and around the world.”

item.title: 1 GW solar capacity reaches FID in Q3 2026, a confident CER boosts 2027 projection
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Following a record 5 GW of large-scale renewable energy investment to the end of Q3 2026, the Clean Energy Regulator has raised the lower bound of its 2026-2027 FID projection from 6 GW-8 GW, up to 8 GW-16 GW.
item.content:encoded:
Following a record 5 GW of large-scale renewable energy investment to the end of Q3 2026, up from 4.9 GW in 2025, the Clean Energy Regulator (CER) has raised the lower bound of its 2026-2027 final investment decision (FID) projection from 6 GW-8 GW, to 8 GW-16 GW.

“In the Q4 2025 Quarterly Carbon Market Report (QCMR), we projected that between 6 and 16 GW of large-scale renewable generation capacity would reach FID over 2026 and 2027. The record level of investment activity observed during 2026 has significantly reduced downside risks to this outlook,” the Q3 2026 QCMR report says.

Of the nine projects to reach FID in Q3 2026 totalling 2.1 GW, five received support under the Capacity Investment Scheme (CIS) including two solar projects in Queensland, the 150 MW Ganymirra Solar Power Station and 150 MW Majors Creek Solar Farm.

It was the fourth-strongest quarter for solar with 1 GW of capacity reaching FID. By mid-November 2026 all investments moved year-to-date FID to 5.5 GW.

“Solar accounted for 3.5 GW of FID in 2026 to date,” the report says. “Australian Renewable Energy Agency’s (ARENA) update to their Ultra Low-cost Solar white paper identified a range of opportunities to reduce the cost of deploying utility-scale solar in Australia, which could continue to strengthen the investment case for both standalone solar and hybrid solar-and-storage projects.”

The report also says the ARENA paper highlights improved cell and module efficiency, innovation in construction and deployment models, including automation, prefabrication, modular delivery, and digital and data-driven operational and maintenance optimisation as potential pathways to lower project costs.

Battery pipeline

The CER’s new large-scale battery pipeline tracker recorded 3.4 GW and 13.8 GWh of storage capacity reaching FID in Q3, taking the 2026 total to date to 5.1 GW and 20 GWh, where average capacity more than doubled from 265 MWh in 2025 to 621 MWh in the year so far.

Projects to reach FID included the 2,200 MWh Richmond Valley Solar Farm BESS in New South Wales (NSW), and the 1,860 MWh Baranduda Electrical Energy Reserve and 1,200 MWh Moorabool Battery, both in Victoria.

In Queensland, the 1,215 MWh Stage 3 South Pine Supernode BESS and 800 MWh Koolunga BESS, supported by the CIS, in South Australia (SA).

The QCMR cites the Australian Electricity Market Operator (AEMO) as reporting that average large-scale battery discharge also more than tripled year-on-year and that large-scale batteries set prices in a record 48% of National Electricity Market (NEM) dispatch intervals.

The increased battery charging and changing demand patterns were also attributed to few negative-price intervals and allowed more available large-scale solar generation to be used.

“The share of available solar generation reduced by solar farms in response to low prices (economic offloading) fell by 54% year-on-year while batteries supplied more evening peak generation (8%) than gas (1.5%) for the first time in any quarter,” the report says.

The CER says approvals of renewable generation projects under the Large-scale renewable energy target (LRET) was “subdued”, which it said is expected to lag the recent uplift in investment.

“A total of 0.6 GW was approved in Q3, bringing approvals to 2.1 GW for the year-to-date. With 570 MW under assessment as 30 September, we have revised our 2026 approvals from project from 3.5 to 4.5 GW to 2.6 to 3.4 GW,” the report says.

item.title: Proposed 8 GWh BESS project in NSW backed by $1.4 billion investment
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Squadron Energy has lodged a scoping report for its proposed $1.5 billion 8 GWh battery energy storage system in New South Wales.
item.content:encoded:
Sydney-headquartered renewable energy company Squadron Energy has lodged a scoping report for its proposed $1.4 billion (USD 980 million) 8 GWh battery energy storage system (BESS) in New South Wales (NSW).

To be located approximately 25 kilometres north of Lithgow, or 170 kilometres northwest of Sydney, the designated State Significant 1 GW / 8,000 MWh Cullen Bullen Battery, has a nominal duration of 8 hours.

A new substation would be constructed to facilitate a connection to NSW high voltage electricity transmission manager Transgrid’s existing onsite overhead 500 kV transmission network.

In early stages of development, Squadron is seeking feedback from the local community to inform the total 660-hectare project’s design and build.

Squadron Energy Project Developer Sean Cross said engaging with the community early and delivering lasting local benefits are priorities for Squadron.

“Squadron is committed to delivering real benefits for local families and businesses through investment in infrastructure, funding for community programs and the creation of local jobs and training opportunities,” Cross said.

“We’re already investing in the local community through our sponsorship program, with funding available to support organisations delivering education and training, community development, health and wellbeing, and environmental initiatives.”

A NSW Department of Planning Secretary’s environmental assessment requirements (SEARs) is expected to be issued in December 2026 and detailed design and construction by 2029, pending necessary approvals, with construction likely in 2030.

The project would be situated 1.1 kilometres northwest of Alinta Energy’s proposed 500 MW wind farm and 200 MW / 800 MWh BESS, 7.8 kilometres southwest from Someva Renewables and Mainstream Renewable Power’s proposed 500 MW wind farm, and 8.1 kilometres southeast from EnergyAustralia’s approved 500 MW / 2 GWh BESS.

Within a 25 kilometre radius of the Cullen Bullen Battery would be the approved 500 MW / 1 GWh Neoen Great Western BESS and the 600 MW Shell Energy Wallerawang BESS, and the proposed 700 MW / 2.8 GWh Centennial Coal Ivanhoe BESS, plus other clean energy projects.

item.title: Untapped transmission capacity freed by dynamic battery load-sharing: report
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: A new report from the IEEFA shows coordinated multiple battery reserves could unlock underutilised transmission capacity, pointing to a flexible BESS-SIPS portfolio that could can extend existing big battery support of transmission networks.
item.content:encoded:
A new report from the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) shows coordinated multiple battery reserves could unlock underutilised transmission capacity, saying a flexible battery energy storage (BESS)-system integrity protection scheme (SIPS) portfolio can build on existing big battery support of transmission networks.

Designed to meet the increased uptake in consumer electrification and data centre connections, the report says a Flexible BESS-SIPS Portfolio could have the potential to keep pace with increasing renewable energy connections to the National Electricity Market (NEM), which currently outpace transmission projects by up to eight years.

The IEEFA ‘Dynamic battery reserves can deliver network benefits’ Report Author and Engineer Dr Sarah Probert says that while new generation and load connections have delivery timeframes typically of two to three years, transmission projects are much longer.

“The sequencing gap between connections and transmission development increases the risk of energy supply limitations and high electricity prices arising from insufficient transmission capacity,” Probert says in the report.

Highlighting the Victorian Big Battery and Waratah Super Battery transmission supports under existing SIPS contracts, and the Waratah contract being more flexible to improve utilisation, the report recommends a broader Flexible BESS–SIPS Portfolio to extend these services.

Coordinating multiple batteries across corridors could provide rapid fault response, slow resecuring support, or both, and enable transmission lines to run at higher levels, unlocking more renewable energy from renewable energy zones (REZs).

Probert recommends the concept be tested through modelling and a system trial that tests feasibility, costs, battery locations, transfer uplift, and the frequency and duration of reserve needs.

The initial procurement could use tenders or existing network and transitional-service contracts, with a dedicated mechanism for later consideration, Probert recommends.

Probert says a new System Operator function should be established to co-ordinate the Flexible BESS–SIPS Portfolio.

The System Operator could identify when additional reserves are required, particularly during periods of high REZ generation, high demand or planned outages, and optimise the quantity and type of reserve response from any participating BESS.

“This function would support greater utilisation of existing transmission infrastructure and facilitate higher levels of renewable energy transfer,” Probert says.

“The Australian Energy Market Commission (AEMC) should consider the benefits of standalone BESS and hybrid systems delivering a Flexible BESS–SIPS Portfolio response to increase network capacity as part of its Electricity Network Regulation Review.”

item.title: UNSW, UtmoLight achieve 19.6% efficiency for 2.81 m² perovskite solar module
item.dc:creator: Vincent Shaw
item.description: The reported result corresponds to a power output of around 551 W and represents a 15% relative efficiency increase over UtmoLight’s previous benchmark. The module was tested at Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese perovskite solar module manufacturer UtmoLight and researchers from the University of New South Wales (UNSW) Sydney have reportedly achieved a stabilised power conversion efficiency of 19.6% for a single-junction perovskite solar module measuring 2.81 m².

According to technical documentation seen by pv magazine, the result was obtained through maximum power point tracking (MPPT) tests conducted at Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems (Fraunhofer ISE).

The reported full-area efficiency corresponds to a power output of approximately 551 W under standard test conditions.

The result represents an improvement of 2.56 percentage points over UtmoLight’s previous efficiency benchmark for modules of comparable size, equivalent to a relative efficiency increase of around 15%.

Maintaining high power conversion efficiencies while increasing module size remains one of the main challenges in the commercialisation of perovskite photovoltaics. Large-area module fabrication requires precise control of thin-film uniformity, crystallisation, defect passivation, electrical interconnections, and interface quality.

The collaboration combines UNSW’s expertise in materials science and device engineering with UtmoLight’s large-area processing and industrial manufacturing capabilities.

Earlier this year, the two partners achieved a certified stabilised efficiency of 23.5% for a 30 cm × 30 cm single-junction perovskite solar submodule with an aperture area of 676 cm².

The researchers eliminated the conventional nickel oxide layer through a fabrication process that enables the direct formation of a hole-selective contact.

The UNSW team subsequently announced plans to scale up the technology to a module area of 2.8 m², targeting a power conversion efficiency of between 18% and 19%.

UtmoLight has been working on the development of commercial-sized perovskite solar modules for several years. In November 2024, the company unveiled a 450 W perovskite solar panel with a power conversion efficiency of 16.1%, an area of 2.8 m², and a dual-glass design.

In February 2025, it began production at its GW-scale perovskite solar module factory in Wuxi, in China’s Jiangsu province.

A month later, the manufacturer achieved a stabilised full-area efficiency of 18.1% for a 0.72 m² perovskite solar module with a power output of 130.5 W. The device was fabricated on the company’s 150 MW pilot production line, with the results confirmed by the US National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL).

In May 2025, TÜV Rheinland reportedly confirmed a stabilised power output of 480.5 W and a full-area efficiency of 17.04% for a 2.82 m² module developed by the Chinese manufacturer.

UtmoLight has also been working to improve the mechanical durability of its products. At the SNEC trade show in Shanghai in June 2026, the company introduced two new perovskite solar modules targeting different deployment scenarios.

Its 500 W Chuangshi S2 module measures 2.81 m² and features a dual-glass design incorporating 3.2 mm tempered glass. The panel passed front- and rear-side mechanical load tests of 5,400 Pa and 2,400 Pa, respectively.

The company also unveiled the Chuangshi S1, a lightweight 0.72 m² perovskite solar module weighing 4 kg and designed for building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV) and rooftops with limited load-bearing capacity.

UtmoLight is targeting a power conversion efficiency of 20% in mass production.

item.title: Envision strikes renewable hydrogen agreement to power green steel
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Greensteel Australia and Chinese multinational Envision Energy have partnered to explore the development of a 400 MW green hydrogen system and integrated renewable energy supply to power low-carbon iron and steelmaking in New South Wales.
item.content:encoded:
Sydney-based Greensteel Australia said it has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Envision Energy to explore an initial 400 MW green hydrogen system to power a new all-electric steel mill to be built in the New South Wales (NSW) Hunter region.

Greensteel has committed $500 million (USD 332 million) to build what would be the first new steel mill in Australia for more than 30 years at the site of the disused BHP steelworks at Mayfield North near Newcastle.

The plant is expected to be up and running by early 2028 and will use renewable electricity and electric arc furnace (EAF) technology to produce up to 600,000 tonnes of finished steel annually.

Greensteel said the direct reduced iron (DRI) plant is being designed to operate using green hydrogen instead of coking coal, one of the most important steps toward producing steel with dramatically lower emissions.

“Our ambition is to build a stronger, more integrated steel industry in Australia,” Greensteel Chief Executive Officer Romany Ibrahim said. “While Mayfield focuses on domestic steel processing, the next stage extends the value chain upstream into low-carbon ironmaking and steel production.”

Greensteel said it will now work with Envision to look at the integration of renewable electricity, energy storage, hydrogen production and industrial demand, as well as opportunities for shared infrastructure, resource recovery and the utilisation of industrial by-products.

The collaboration will cover regional wind and solar integration, grid connectivity, energy storage, hydrogen production and industrial load management, alongside system configuration, operating strategies and phased development. 

Greensteel said Shanghai-headquartered Envision, which specialises in green hydrogen solutions, wind turbines, and battery energy storage systems, brings “proven green hydrogen technology and operating experience, along with expertise in wind, solar and energy storage.”

The two parties have said beyond green steel, the partnership will also explore local manufacturing of renewable energy infrastructure, including steel structures, wind turbine tower components, foundations, anchoring components and precast concrete.

Envision Senior Vice President and Chief Product Officer Yimin Lou said the company will work with Greensteel and potential local partners to assess technical suitability, market demand and commercial viability.

“Green hydrogen’s strategic value goes beyond energy substitution. Integrating it with downstream industry can create a globally competitive industrial ecosystem,” he said. “Through this collaboration, we aim to combine Envision’s wind, solar, energy storage, green hydrogen and net-zero industrial systems expertise with Greensteel Australia’s local ambitions to establish a practical, scalable model for green industrial transformation.”

item.title: US solar robotics company pushes on with Australian manufacturing plans
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Luminous Robotics expects the first of at least 100 Australian-made autonomous solar panel installation robots will roll out of its new $39.7 million manufacturing facility in Melbourne by mid-2027.
item.content:encoded:
United States-based robotics company Luminous Robotics is progressing plans to establish production facilities in Melbourne where it will manufacture a fleet of robots designed to accelerate utility-scale solar deployment and reduce construction costs.

Luminous has developed a specialised robotics fleet that includes two complementary platforms designed to automate solar panel installation on large-scale solar farms. The company’s architecture includes the Pallet Lumi v2, a robotic platform that transports solar panels along the installation row, and the Install Lumi that collects the panels individually and places them onto the mounting structure.

The company said its current generation of automated robot allows for solar panels to be installed with a cycle time as low as 40 seconds.

Luminous Australia General Manager Tenzin Crouch said the application of coordinated robotics system has already been successfully trialled at large-scale solar builds in Victoria and New South Wales (NSW) and the company is now looking to scale up manufacturing.

“We have proven that these robots do work in Australia, doing some of the hardest work on site,” he said. “The next step is to turn that into scale.”

Luminous is planning to establish a $39.7 million manufacturing facility, backed by $17.8 million from Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA), in Melbourne with Crouch confirming he expects to sign the lease for a factory site in the coming weeks. Fit-out will begin in early 2027, with production starting in the second quarter.

“We’ll establish that facility Q1 next year and have first robots off the production line Q2 next year,” he said, adding that the project is expected to deliver about 100 pallet and install Lumi robots by 2029.

“We have an initial production run of five robots by mid-year next year,” he said. “And then from there, that facility is targeted to produce about 15 robots every six months across both generations of the pallet and the plate installation.”

Crouch said the Lumi platform takes on the heavy, repetitive work of lifting and placing solar panels with the current generation of robots up to 2.5 times faster than existing labour practices. The company is working towards about a four times efficiency, unlocking the potential to significantly lower solar farm construction costs.

“And because the machines are electric, that would allow for overnight operations which would be a game-changer,” Crouch said, adding the shift towards commercial-scale local manufacturing is the opportunity to take robots already working alongside Australian solar crews and build them at a scale that matches the work ahead.

“There’s approximately 160 GW of projects in Australia’s development pipeline,” he said. “Even if 50% of them don’t get through DA, there’s still 80 GW over the next 10 years so there’s a lot to do.”

In addition to the Australian market, Luminous sees the Melbourne facility as a potential base to serve New Zealand, South America and Southeast Asia.

“We see Australia as a sort of export hub for the region,” Crouch said. “New Zealand is not a huge market but it’s quite growing quite a lot, Chile as well, and then obviously up into Southeast Asia.”

Luminous said the Lumi robots will be assembled and tested at the Melbourne facility, with Australian suppliers fabricating metal parts from the outset. As the fleet grows, the company will look to bring more local suppliers into production.

“It is going to start mostly as assembly, but our intent is to over the course of the project onshore a lot of the fabrication aspects of that as well,” Crouch said. “So the local supply chain is going to level up.”
